Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "Social-affective features drive human representations of observed actions" for further consideration by eLife. Your revised article has been evaluated by Chris Baker (Senior Editor) in consultation with the original reviewers.

We all agree the manuscript has been improved, the issues raised by the reviewers have been addressed well, and the manuscript will make a nice addition to the literature. But one of the reviewers highlighted a remaining concern that I wanted to draw your attention to. This concern could be addressed with additional analyses or additional discussion and motivation of the approach you used (I will leave it up to you which avenue you want to pursue). I'll quote from the reviewer:

"Among the visual features the authors investigate is motion. To me, this is a visual feature that would seem to have a strong potential to explain the EEG data in particular, since motion contrast strongly drives many visual areas. I am not completely satisfied with the way the authors have quantified motion, and I have a medium concern that their motion model is a bit of a straw man. First, they refer to the model as a "motion energy" model, which is not technically correct. Motion energy (i.e. Adelson and Bergen, 1985; Nishimoto et al., 2011) reflects image contrast, whereas optic flow does not (at least to the same degree). For example, a gray square moving 2 degrees on a slightly less gray background will generate the same magnitudes of optic flow vectors as a starkly black square on a white background moving the same distance. Motion energy will be substantially greater for higher-contrast stimuli. As such, it's likely that motion energy would be a better model for visual responses (at least in early visual areas) than optic flow. They also choose to compute optic flow densely, with one value per pixel. Thus, if actors in the various videos are in slightly different locations, the optic flow metric could be quite different, and the RDM may characterize arguably similar stimuli as distinct. I think that a multi-scale pyramid of optic flow (or better still, motion energy) would have a better chance of capturing motion selectivity in the way that the brain does.

There is one more choice that the authors make that I'm not entirely comfortable with, which relates to this same issue. They choose to use only the models that can be related to behavioral data to model the EEG data. This choice is motivated by the desire to relate brain activity to behavior, which is a worthwhile endeavor. However, I think there is an assumption underlying this choice: the authors assume that the signal that they measure with EEG must reflect neural representations that guide behavior and not low-level perceptual processes. I do not think that this is guaranteed to be the case. EEG measures a spatially diffuse signal, which may well be dominated by activity from quite low-level areas (e.g. V1). I think the question of whether the EEG signal reflects relatively high-level cognitive processing or relatively low-level perceptual processing – for any given experiment – is still open. For most of the models they exclude, I don't think this is a big issue. For example, I think it's reasonable to test luminance basically as a control (to show that there aren't huge differences in luminance that can explain behavior) and then to exclude it from the EEG modeling. However, I'm less happy with exclusion of motion, based on a somewhat sub-optimal motion model not explaining behavior.

The combination of these two issues has left me wanting a better quantification of motion as a model for the EEG data. My bet would be that motion would be a decent model for the EEG signal at an earlier stage than they see the effects of action class and social factors in the signal, so I don't necessarily think that modeling motion would be likely to eliminate the effects they do see; to my mind, it would just present a fairer picture of what's going on with the EEG signal."

results.result: Two stimulus sets were created containing 152 and 65 videos respectively, representing 18 common activities from the American Time Use Survey. Multiple behavioral experiments were conducted with participants from Amazon Mechanical Turk and Johns Hopkins University, along with an EEG experiment, all with appropriate ethical approval.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C4 provide clear descriptions of the stimulus sets with specific numbers that are internally consistent. Claims C66-C71 document participant recruitment and ethical approvals with specific protocol numbers. These methodological details are straightforward and well-documented.

results.result: 17 visual, action-related, and social-affective features were quantified using image properties, experimenter labels, and behavioral ratings. Visual features ranged from low-level to high-level, action features included transitivity, activity, effectors, and action category, and social-affective features included sociality, valence, arousal, and number of agents. Representational dissimilarity matrices (RDMs) were created for each feature.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C72-C76 describe the feature quantification methodology in detail. The approach is clearly documented with specific feature types listed. The creation of RDMs using Euclidean distances is a standard method in representational similarity analysis.

results.result: Visual features were minimally correlated with action/social-affective features in both video sets, and the distributions of action and social-affective features were not significantly different between the two stimulus sets.
results.evaluation: Claims C11 and C13 report correlation analyses and statistical tests (Mann-Whitney z < 1.08, p>0.28) with appropriate statistical reporting. Figure 1a provides visual evidence supporting the minimal correlation claim. The statistical test for distribution comparison is appropriate.

results.result: Behaviorally rated features differed in reliability in Experiment 1 (F(4,819) = 22.35, p<0.001), with sociality being most reliable and arousal least reliable, but there was no difference in reliability in Experiment 2 (F(4,619) = 0.76, p=0.55).
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C15 report ANOVA results with appropriate F-statistics, degrees of freedom, and p-values. The difference between experiments is clearly stated with statistical support. Figure 3—figure supplement 1 provides supporting evidence.

results.result: Participants arranged videos according to similarity in a multiple arrangement task without specific criteria. Behavioral RDMs were reconstructed using inverse MDS. Experiment 1 took 32±14.4 min with 86.8±22.6 trials and contained 11,476 pairs with 11.37±3.08 estimates per pair. Experiment 2 took 87.5±24.6 min with 289.7±57.3 trials and contained 2080 pairs arranged by all 53 participants.
results.evaluation: Claims C16, C77-C82 provide detailed methodological information about the multiple arrangement task with specific quantitative measures. The use of inverse MDS is a standard approach (C78 cites Kriegeskorte and Mur, 2012). The experimental parameters are clearly documented.

results.result: Reliability was significantly higher in Experiment 2 than in Experiment 1 (Mann-Whitney z = 3.21, p=0.0013), potentially reflecting differences in participant pools and sampling methods.
results.evaluation: Claim C18 reports a statistical comparison with appropriate test (Mann-Whitney) and significant p-value. The interpretation about potential causes is appropriately qualified as speculative. The statistical test is appropriate for comparing two independent groups.

results.result: In Experiment 1, only two visual features (environment and FC8 of AlexNet) were significantly correlated with behavioral RDMs, while all action-related and social-affective RDMs showed significant correlations. In Experiment 2, only effectors and activity among action features were significantly correlated, but all social-affective features showed significant correlations.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C23 report correlation results that are visualized in Figure 3. The pattern of results is consistent across both experiments showing stronger correlations for social-affective features. The statistical significance is appropriately assessed (p<0.005, sign permutation testing as noted in Figure 3).

results.result: Ten features that contributed significantly to behavior in either experiment were selected for variance partitioning analysis, with no collinearity among predictors (average VIF of 1.34 in Experiment 1 and 1.37 in Experiment 2).
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C25 describe the feature selection process and report variance inflation factors to assess collinearity. VIF values below 2 indicate minimal collinearity, supporting the validity of the variance partitioning approach. This is appropriate methodological practice.

results.result: Social-affective features predicted similarity judgments better than, and independently of, visual and action features in both behavioral experiments. In both experiments, social-affective features contributed significantly more unique variance than visual or action features (all Wilcoxon z > 5.5, p<0.001). In Experiment 1, all three groups contributed unique variance (all p<0.001), but in Experiment 2, only social-affective features contributed significantly (p<0.001). Social-affective features explained more than twice as much unique variance in Experiment 1 and six times as much in Experiment 2.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C26-C30 report the main behavioral finding with appropriate statistical tests (Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, randomization testing) and effect sizes. Figure 4 provides clear visualization. The cross-validated variance partitioning approach is rigorous. The replication across two experiments strengthens the finding.

results.result: Control analyses showed that replacing action category with WordNet RDM did not increase variance explained by action features, a motion energy model correlated with behavior in Experiment 1 but not Experiment 2, adding motion energy did not change the pattern of unique feature contributions, and social-affective features explained significantly more variance than all other features grouped together.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C34 report control analyses that test alternative explanations and validate the main findings. The results are shown in supplementary figures (Figure 4—figure supplements 1-3). These analyses strengthen the main conclusion by ruling out alternative explanations.

results.result: Higher-level social-affective features (sociality, valence, and arousal) contributed more unique variance than the number of agents in both experiments, with affective features (valence and arousal) contributing the greatest variance.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C36 report additional variance partitioning analyses that dissect the social-affective feature group. The results are shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 4-5. These analyses demonstrate that the effect is not driven solely by the number of agents (a potentially more visual feature).

results.result: In the EEG experiment, participants viewed 500 ms video segments and performed a one-back action task. EEG was recorded at 1000 Hz using a 64-channel system. The experiment consisted of 1720 trials and took approximately 45 min. After preprocessing, 13.74±1.82% of trials were removed for button responses and 8.36±5.01% for artifacts. Time-resolved decoding was performed using linear SVM with split-half cross-validation, repeated 10 times.
results.evaluation: Claims C37, C83-C90 provide detailed EEG methodology with specific parameters. The preprocessing steps are standard for EEG analysis. The decoding approach using split-half cross-validation is appropriate. The trial exclusion rates are reasonable and clearly documented.

results.result: Decoding accuracy rose above chance at 50 ms after video onset, reached its maximum at 98 ms (63.88±6.82% accuracy), and remained above chance until 852 ms after video onset (cluster-corrected p<0.05).
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C40 report the time course of decoding accuracy with specific timing and accuracy values. The statistical testing uses appropriate cluster correction for multiple comparisons. The results are consistent with prior EEG/MEG studies as noted in the manuscript.

results.result: An EEG experiment revealed a sustained correlation between neural responses to videos and their behavioral similarity during a cluster between 62 and 766 ms after video onset, suggesting that features guiding intuitive categorization also underlie neural organization.
results.evaluation: Claims C7 and C41 report the brain-behavior correlation with specific timing (62-766 ms) and appropriate statistical testing (cluster-corrected). Figure 5b visualizes this result. The interpretation that behaviorally relevant features underlie neural organization is supported by the correlation.

results.result: Visual predictors correlated with neural patterns between 65±15ms (Conv1) and 84±62ms (Environment), action category had an early onset (58±9ms), other action features emerged later (transitivity: 170±67ms, effectors: 192±94ms, activity: 345±133ms), and among social-affective features, number of agents emerged earliest (178±81ms) while valence and arousal emerged later (395±81 and 404±91ms).
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C46 report bootstrapping analysis results for correlation onsets with means and standard deviations. Figure 5c visualizes these results with 90% confidence intervals. The temporal progression from visual to action to social-affective features is clearly demonstrated.

results.result: Visual, action, and social-affective features predicted neural patterns at early, intermediate, and late stages respectively. Visual features dominated early time windows (66-138ms), action features contributed unique variance (162-598ms) and shared variance with social-affective features (354-598ms), and social-affective features independently predicted late responses (446-782ms). Visual features did not share significant variance with other features. Social-affective features (onset 418±89ms) contributed unique variance significantly later than action features (245±104ms), which came online later than visual features (65±8ms; all Wilcoxon z > 7.27, p<0.001).
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C47-C53 report the main EEG finding of a temporal hierarchy with specific time windows and statistical tests. Figure 6 provides clear visualization. The variance partitioning approach with cross-validation is rigorous. The statistical comparisons of onsets are appropriate (Wilcoxon tests). The finding of independent contributions from each feature group is well-supported.

results.result: Motion energy correlated with EEG patterns beginning at 62ms. Adding motion energy increased visual feature contributions and decreased action feature contributions, but the three-stage temporal hierarchy was preserved in fixed-effects analysis, and the unique contribution of social-affective features was unchanged.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C57 report control analyses with motion energy shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3. The finding that motion energy shares variance with action features is interpretable, and the preservation of the temporal hierarchy and social-affective contribution strengthens the main conclusion.

results.result: Sociality did not correlate with EEG patterns, and this absence was not likely driven by lower reliability in measurement, as sociality was more reliable than all other behaviorally rated features in Experiment 1.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C92 report a null finding with appropriate consideration of measurement reliability. The reasoning that rules out reliability as an explanation is sound. However, the absence of an effect should be interpreted cautiously, as noted by the authors' discussion of potential confounds with other features.

results.result: Features emerged spontaneously as the one-back task only related to action category, which is not correlated with any other features in the dataset, suggesting the temporal hierarchy would emerge in the absence of a task.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C94 make an inference about spontaneous feature extraction and speculate about task-independence. While the reasoning is plausible, the manuscript acknowledges that semantic processing required for the task may have contributed, and explicitly states that future work is needed to test this directly. The claim about action category not correlating with other features needs verification against Figure 1a.

results.result: Social-affective features are important for perceiving naturalistic actions and are extracted at the final stage of a temporal gradient in the brain. Visual feature extraction occurs rapidly within 200ms via feedforward computations. The final social-affective stage was reflected in intuitive behavioral representations. Action-related features were extracted significantly before social-affective features, suggesting hierarchical rather than parallel processing. Social-affective features may result from ongoing processing relying on temporal integration of previously extracted features.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C10, C95-C98 synthesize the main findings and provide interpretations. The conclusions about importance of social-affective features and temporal hierarchy are well-supported by the combined behavioral and neural data (C6, C8, C26-C30, C47-C53). The interpretation about feedforward processing for visual features is consistent with the timing. The speculation about temporal integration (C98) is appropriately qualified as possible rather than definitive.

results.result: The seemingly conflicting features revealed by previous studies (number of agents, sociality, semantic action category) emerge at different stages during action observation. The existence of different organizing dimensions can be explained through a temporal gradient starting with visual features and concluding with behaviorally relevant social and affective representations.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C100 provide an integrative interpretation that reconciles prior conflicting findings through the temporal dynamics revealed in this study. This interpretation is well-supported by the data showing different features emerge at different times (C42-C46, C47-C53) and is appropriately cited to relevant prior work.

results.result: Prior work has established that viewpoint-invariant responses emerge by 200ms, biological motion is extracted within 200ms in superior temporal cortex, occipito-temporal areas reflect semantic and social features, naturalistic datasets improve ecological validity, context modulates neural activity, and previous studies have yielded conflicting results about whether sociality or semantic action category is the primary organizing dimension.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C65, C101-C102 summarize prior work with appropriate citations. These claims provide context for the current study and are standard literature review statements. The citations appear appropriate for the claims made.
